In this application exercise we will be studying penguins.
The data can be found in the **palmerpenguins** package and we will use **tidyverse** and **tidymodels** for data exploration and modeling, respectively.

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

Read the following context and take a `glimpse` at the data set before we get started.

> This data set comprising various measurements of three different penguin species, namely Adelie, Gentoo, and Chinstrap.
> The rigorous study was conducted in the islands of the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica.
> These data were collected from 2007 to 2009 by Dr. Kristen Gorman with the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research Program, part of the US Long Term Ecological Research Network.
> The data set is called `penguins`.

```{r}
#| label: glimpse-penguins
glimpse(penguins)
```

## Visualizing the relationship

Our goal is to understand better how various body measurements and attributes of penguins relate to their body mass.

- Create an appropriate plot to investigate the relationship between penguins' flipper length and body mass. Put the predictor on the x-axis and the outcome on the y-axis. Add appropriate labels.

```{r}
#| label: visualize
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    title = "Body mass vs. flipper length",
    subtitle = "Palmer penguins"
  )
```

- Describe the **form, direction, and strength** of the relationship. Note any unusual observations.

*The relationship is roughly linear, positive, and strong: penguins with higher
flipper lengths tend to have higher body mass. There are no unusual observations.*

- Let R draw the regression line. Use `geom_smooth()` with `method = "lm"` and set `se = FALSE`.

```{r}
#| label: visualize-with-line
#| warning: false
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    title = "Body mass vs. flipper length",
    subtitle = "Palmer penguins"
  )
```

- What types of questions can this plot help answer?

*How does penguin body mass tend to change with flipper length? What body mass
would we predict for a penguin with a given flipper length?*

## Model fit and summary

- Fit a linear regression model that predicts body mass from flipper length.

```{r}
#| label: fit-model

bm_fl_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguins)

bm_fl_fit
```

- Display the model summary and extract the slope and intercept estimates.

```{r}
#| label: model-summary
tidy(bm_fl_fit)
```

- Write the fitted model using mathematical notation.

$$
\widehat{body~mass} = -5781 + 49.7 \times flipper~length
$$


- Interpret the slope in context.

*For each additional millimeter of a penguin's flipper length, their predicted weight will be higher, on average, by 49.7 grams.*

- Interpret the intercept in context. Is this interpretation meaningful for these data?

*Penguins with a flipper length of 0 are predicted to weigh -5781 grams. This is the mathematical interpretation, but it is not practically meaningful: penguins cannot have a flipper length of zero, nor a negative mass!*

## Correlation

- Calculate the correlation between flipper length and body mass. Interpret its sign and magnitude.

```{r}
#| label: correlation
penguins |>
  summarize(r = cor(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, use = "complete.obs"))
```

*The correlation is approximately 0.871, indicating a strong positive linear relationship.*

## Predictions and residuals

- Use the model to predict the body mass of a penguin with a flipper length of 210mm.

```{r}
#| label: prediction
new_penguin <- tibble(flipper_length_mm = 210)

predict(bm_fl_fit, new_data = new_penguin)
```

*The predicted mass is approximately 4653g.*

- If appropriate, use the model to predict the body mass of a penguin with a flipper length of 100mm.

*This prediction isn't appropriate since 100 mm is outside of the range of the data (extrapolation).*

- Use `augment()` to add predictions and residuals to the penguins data.

```{r}
#| label: augment-model
penguins_aug <- augment(
  bm_fl_fit,
  new_data = penguins
)
penguins_aug
```

# Linear regression with a categorical predictor

-   A different researcher wants to look at body weight of penguins based on the island they were recorded on. How are the variables involved in this analysis different?

*Predictor is categorical.*

-   Make an appropriate visualization to investigate this relationship below. Additionally, calculate the mean body mass by island.

```{r}
#| label: plot-bm-island
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

```{r}
#| label: mean-bm-island
penguins |>
  group_by(island) |>
  summarize(mean_bm = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
```

-   Fit the linear regression model and display the results. Write the model below.

```{r}
#| label: fit-bm-island
bm_island_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(body_mass_g ~ island, data = penguins)

tidy(bm_island_fit)
```

$$\widehat{bodymass} = 4716 - 1003*islandDream -1010*islandTorgersen$$

-   Interpret each coefficient in the context of the problem.

    -   Intercept: The model predicts penguins from Biscoe to weigh 4716 grams.

    -   Slopes:

        -   The model predicts penguins from Dream island to weigh, on average, 1003 grams less than those from Biscoe island.

        -   The model predicts penguins from Torgersen island to weigh, on average, 1010 grams less than those from Biscoe island.

-   What is the estimated body weight of a penguin on Biscoe island?
    What are the estimated body weights of penguins on Dream and Torgersen islands?

```{r}
#| label: predict-bm-island
three_penguins <- tibble(
  island = c("Biscoe", "Dream", "Torgersen")
)
bm_island_fit |>
  predict(new_data = three_penguins)
```

- Penguins on Biscoe island are estimated to weigh
4716 grams.

- Penguins on Dream Island are estimated to weigh 3713 grams.

- Penguins on Torgersen Island are estimated to weigh
3706 grams.
